title: Pickleball Courts Inside Empty Fellowship Halls
one_liner: A turnkey operator that converts congregations' idle gyms and fellowship halls into revenue-sharing indoor pickleball venues, with lines, nets, insurance and booking handled.
customer: Congregations (churches, synagogues, mosques, temples) with a gym or hall and parking lot, who receive a rent share. Players (often retirees on weekday mornings) pay $8-15 per session.
problem: US pickleball grew from 13.6M (2023) to 24.3M (2025) players, but courts are scarce (about 1 dedicated court per 1,000 participants in the Mid-Atlantic, and about $900M of investment needed per a 2022 SFIA report). Outdoor courts are being restricted or closed by noise complaints. Meanwhile congregations that are shrinking or flat (only 33% of Americans attend monthly) sit on large rooms used a few hours a week, and fear liability and tax surprises.
solution: A standard hall kit (removable court lines, portable nets, wall padding, ball machine), a legal and insurance package (lease template, additional-insured wording, a flat-rent structure designed to avoid UBIT problems, waivers), a booking app with open-play scheduling and rating-linked sessions, and part-time paid hosts. Indoor play removes the neighbor-noise problem.
why_now: Participation more than doubled in two years, and noise fights are closing outdoor courts (Kirkwood MO, Walnut Creek CA, Halifax). Church rental-liability gaps are a known insurance pain point. Congregations need non-donation income.
revenue_model: Player fees of $10-14 per session. The congregation takes a 20-40% share and the operator keeps the rest less host cost. Kit rental or sale ($200/month or $3-5k) and an insurance-program commission.
non_obvious_insight: The court shortage is framed as a construction problem needing $900M. It is a liability and coordination problem: the courts already exist as 40x70 ft hardwood rooms with parking, owned by institutions that want steady income but cannot underwrite risk. A congregation is also a more trusted neighbor than a new commercial club.
first_30_days: Sign 3 congregations with gyms in one metro through denominational property committees and local pickleball Facebook groups. Run two open-play nights a week using a $1.5k kit. Pre-sell via local groups, track fill rate, and get a church-insurer quote. Aim for $1-2k revenue in the first month.

title: Insured Filing Clerk for Multi-City Contractor Licenses
one_liner: A computer-use agent that renews and files contractor and business licenses across city and county portals that have no APIs, backed by a penalty warranty.
customer: Trade contractors (electricians, plumbers, HVAC, roofers, landscapers, painters), mobile groomers, food trucks and short-term-rental hosts working across many cities or counties, with 2-30 employees.
problem: Each city and county has its own business-license, registration and permit portal, fee schedule and renewal date, with COI and bond uploads. Missing one triggers fines or stop-work orders. Enterprise-priced compliance vendors ignore small firms, and payroll vendors are bundling only payroll compliance (Gusto bought Mosey in April 2026).
solution: An agent operates the same portals a human would to renew, upload COIs and bonds, pay fees with a virtual card and capture receipts. Human reviewers verify sensitive steps. A warranty pays penalties for missed or incorrect filings. Every filing improves a jurisdiction knowledge base of forms, fees and quirks.
why_now: Browser and computer-use agents crossed a reliability threshold in 2025-26, and payroll compliance has been productized, leaving licenses and permits as the untouched adjacent layer.
revenue_model: $59/month plus $15 per filing plus fee pass-through, with the warranty cost built into pricing.
non_obvious_insight: With roughly 19,000 municipalities, no API strategy will ever cover the map, but an agent that uses the human interface can. The moat is the jurisdiction graph and the warranty.
first_30_days: Pick a dense metro cluster with many cities and one trade. Assist 20 contractors with renewals, recording each portal flow, and sign a COI and bond partner for bulk uploads. Track error rate and hours saved.

title: Lend Against Battery Earnings for Vet Bills
one_liner: A wallet that routes VPP and demand-response payouts into a dedicated pet-care fund, then advances emergency vet money against the battery's telemetry-verified future earnings.
customer: Home-battery owners in VPPs (repayment via payout offset). Partners who pay are VPP aggregators and retail energy providers (retention) and pet insurers (customer acquisition).
problem: Vet bills are lumpy and emotional: 85% of vet professionals say clients decline care at estimates of $1,000 or less, and 13% of euthanasias are attributed to inability to pay. Only about 5% of US dogs and cats are insured, while premiums rose 19.7% against 9% growth in insured animals, which invites churn. High-APR deferred-interest cards are the fallback. Meanwhile VPP payouts are small, abstract and easily ignored, even though dispatch is real (580 MW from 140,000 California batteries on September 9, 2026).
solution: Owners assign payouts to a Pet Reserve that auto-pays insurance premiums and pre-funds vet bills at partner clinics. Once the balance builds, they can draw an advance repaid from future dispatch payments, underwritten on battery telemetry and contracted programs. Start with credits and premium payments only, and add advances through a bank or lender partner once the data is proven.
why_now: VPPs are now large enough to have contracted, metered payout streams (Base Power raised $1B with a 500+ MWh fleet; Sunrun/Tesla dispatch). Pet insurance repricing is pushing owners to look for offsets, and no aggregator owns a consumer-finance layer.
revenue_model: Referral bounty from pet insurers ($50-150 per policy), retention/SaaS fee from aggregators or retailers, and interest or fee spread on repayable advances via a lending partner.
non_obvious_insight: A battery in a VPP is a telemetry-verified income stream, and it is collateralizable. Converting abstract kWh payouts into 'vet visits' also changes how much owners value flexibility, and the pet emergency is the highest-emotion, lowest-friction use of the credit.
first_30_days: Recruit one small VPP operator or retail energy provider (not Tesla) and 300-500 pet-owning households through battery-owner communities. Launch payout-to-Pet-Fund with premium auto-pay and a referral deal with one insurer. Measure opt-in, retention and how many households use the balance for vet bills. Hold advances until a lending partner and legal review are in place.

title: Practice-in-a-Box for Licensed Paraprofessionals
one_liner: Turn displaced paralegals into licensed legal paraprofessionals who can legally sell AI-leveraged flat-fee services directly to the public in states that now allow it.
customer: Displaced or at-risk paralegals and legal assistants, paying $149-299/month, who serve consumers with family law, landlord-tenant, and limited civil matters in states with limited-license programs (Arizona LP, Utah LPP, Oregon LP, Colorado LLP, Minnesota developing).
problem: AI has pushed the value of routine paralegal tasks toward zero inside law firms, while most low-income people's legal problems get little or no help. Several states created limited licenses for exactly this gap, but the licensed pool is tiny because the path (exams, supervised hours, malpractice insurance, trust accounting, client acquisition, tooling) is costly and lonely for a laid-off individual.
solution: A 'practice in a box' with exam and supervised-hours prep, a group malpractice policy, compliant trust accounting, standard intake and scope-check forms, an AI drafting stack with mandatory citation verification and human sign-off, and shared consumer marketing for flat-fee packages (for example, $900 uncontested divorce). It hands off cleanly to lawyers when a matter is out of scope. To respect fee-sharing rules, the company charges flat subscription fees, never a percentage of legal fees.
why_now: Entry-level paralegal roles are among the most cited casualties of 2026 AI layoffs. Colorado's LLP program launched in 2024, Arizona's has licensed since 2021, and Oregon approved its license in 2022. AI drafting makes flat-fee economics finally work for a solo practitioner.
revenue_model: $149-299/month practitioner subscription, exam-prep courses (about $600), group insurance commissions, and per-practitioner advertising placements where permitted.
non_obvious_insight: When AI drives the cost of doing legal work to near zero, the scarce asset is the license to sell it. Regulators created cheap licenses for access-to-justice reasons and they sit underused. Displaced paralegals are the natural supply. The moat is regulatory and operational, not technological.
first_30_days: Pick Arizona and Colorado. Recruit 15 laid-off paralegals through paralegal associations and LinkedIn. Sign a malpractice broker. Launch a $49 'is my matter in scope?' consumer screen as lead generation. Sell exam-prep and onboarding to the first 10 practitioners, about $2k in monthly recurring revenue plus course fees.

title: Hospice for Dying Congregations
one_liner: A managed 'final season' service for congregations that are closing, covering the closing liturgy, an oral-history archive, member placement and a community-first sale of the building.
customer: Denominational regional bodies (dioceses, presbyteries, conferences) and individual congregations with fewer than 50 members deciding to close, and community land trusts and developers who want to reuse their buildings.
problem: Lifeway reported 4,000 Protestant closures against 3,800 openings in 2024, and shrinking, aging congregations keep sliding toward closure. The process is legally messy (deeds, endowments, cemeteries, records, sacred objects) and emotionally painful, and it usually ends in a rushed sale to whoever pays most, with members scattering and often falling out of community altogether.
solution: A 6-12 month managed process: a closing service designed with celebrants, a professional oral-history and photo archive digitised for the community, guided placement of members into neighbouring congregations or community groups, and stewardship of stained glass, organs and memorial gifts. We run a request-for-proposals that favours reuse (housing, community centres) under a mission covenant.
why_now: Post-COVID closures never fully rebounded, clergy are aging, and denominations are sitting on stranded property. California's 2023 law allowing affordable housing on faith-owned land, and the copycat 'YIGBY' bills in other states, make community reuse financially viable.
revenue_model: A fixed fee of roughly $15-40k per congregation paid by the denomination or from sale proceeds, plus a 1-3% success fee on community-reuse sales. Optional licensing of archives to historians, genealogists and local libraries.
non_obvious_insight: Dying congregations do not lack real-estate brokers; they lack a good funeral and a dignified narrative. That is the real barrier to a good sale, because grieving members block anything that feels like betrayal. Whoever holds the funeral earns the trust to shape the outcome toward community use, so you sell a good death and earn the property fee as a consequence.
first_30_days: List 20 congregations flagged for closure in a single denomination region. Offer three subsidised 'Last Sunday' packages at about $5k each, and use the outcomes to pitch the regional executive on a standing contract.

title: Signed Authority Certificates for Buying Agents
one_liner: Companies issue legally strong, machine-verifiable certificates saying which agent may order what, up to what amount, from whom, so suppliers can trust agent-placed orders.
customer: EU industrial distributors and wholesalers that receive purchase orders by email or EDI, and their larger business customers deploying procurement agents. Start with DACH and Benelux distributors.
problem: A supplier gets an order from 'Acme's purchasing agent' and has no way to know it may bind Acme to a EUR 50k purchase. AI makes fake purchase orders and business email compromise cheaper. Consumer-oriented agent-payment mandates (AP2, TAP, Verifiable Intent) do not cover B2B signing authority, and research notes from 2026 say agents do not map cleanly onto EU digital wallet categories.
solution: An authority registry and issuance service. A company's legal representative signs a delegation certificate (qualified electronic signature via eIDAS trust providers, EUDI wallet later) covering agent key, scope (categories or SKUs), per-order and monthly limits, validity and revocation. Suppliers verify by API in under 200 ms and see remaining limit. Integrate with ERP order intake and e-invoicing. The signed record is court-grade evidence in disputes.
why_now: EU member states must offer digital identity wallets by end-2026, financial institutions are expected to accept them by December 2027, and qualified signatures already carry the legal effect of handwritten ones. Agent mandate standards exist but are consumer-centric.
revenue_model: EUR 99-499/month per issuing company, EUR 0.05-0.20 per supplier verification, and enterprise licenses.
non_obvious_insight: Legal effect, not cryptography, is the scarce ingredient in B2B agent commerce. The EU uniquely has an instrument (the qualified signature) that turns a delegation into evidence courts accept, so build where the law already does the hard part.
first_30_days: Integrate with one qualified trust service provider for signing. Interview 20 distributors about agent-placed orders and PO fraud, pilot with 3 distributors and their top buyers on existing order intake, and collect letters of intent.

title: Accessible Council Packets Pipeline
one_liner: An automated pipeline that makes every agenda packet, staff report and PDF a city publishes accessible on arrival, ahead of the ADA Title II deadline.
customer: City and county clerks and IT directors in jurisdictions above 50,000 residents (deadline April 26, 2027), then smaller ones (2028).
problem: Cities publish thousands of legacy PDFs, scanned minutes and meeting packets that fail web accessibility rules. Manual remediation costs $3-10 per page and lawsuits are coming. Staffing is thin, and the deadline is fixed.
solution: Connect to the city's agenda-management and document repository, auto-remediate PDFs (tags, reading order, alt text, tables), route low-confidence pages to human reviewers, and enforce accessible-by-default templates for future documents. Provide the compliance log a city attorney can cite.
why_now: ADA Title II rules set April 2027 for larger jurisdictions and 2028 for smaller ones. GenAI makes remediation of complex documents cheap enough to price against manual work.
revenue_model: $15-80K per year per city depending on volume, plus a backlog cleanup fee ($20-100K one-time).
non_obvious_insight: The recurring stream of new weekly agenda packets, not the legacy backlog, is the durable business. Ship the pipeline at the moment of publishing rather than a one-time remediation project.
first_30_days: Scrape 20 city websites and score their accessibility publicly. Offer free packet remediation for the next council meeting to 5 clerks. Convert on the backlog cleanup quote.

title: Inheriting the Lease: Rent-Stabilized Succession Service
one_liner: A service that helps families of rent-regulated elders build and keep the co-residency evidence that lets them inherit a below-market lease, and files the succession claim within days of a death.
customer: Adult children and relatives living with rent-stabilized or rent-controlled elders (about 1M stabilized units in NYC alone, plus SF, LA, Newark and DC). Elder-law and tenant-rights attorneys, senior centers, home-care agencies and hospital discharge planners white-label or refer.
problem: In regulated housing, a family member who can prove co-residency (typically 2 years, or 1 for seniors and the disabled) can succeed to the lease. The lease can be worth six figures over time. Landlords, who gain by re-renting at market, often contest, and the outcome hinges on documents families never assembled while the elder was alive (IDs, tax returns, bills, benefit and medical mail). After death the family faces a notice in weeks, with the elder's records locked in an unopened estate.
solution: Run a lease-inheritance readiness audit and an evidence ledger that collects only genuine documents (address-bearing IDs, filings, bank and medical mail, affidavits from neighbors). After a death, generate a Day-1 succession packet: notice to the landlord, agency filings, and attorney referral. Contested cases go to partner lawyers on contingency or through right-to-counsel programs.
why_now: NYC's political shift toward tenant protection, the SF rent emergency and record middle-income rent distress raise the stakes. The first Boomer tenants are aging out. Good Cause protections and local rent laws expand the leases worth inheriting. AI-generated pleadings are flooding housing courts, which raises the value of clean, verifiable evidence.
revenue_model: $199-399 per family file plus $6-9 per month for the evidence ledger. White-label and per-file fees from law firms, nonprofits and home-care agencies. Referral fees from partner attorneys.
non_obvious_insight: For many urban middle-class families the biggest asset passed at death is not money but a below-market lease, and the value is lost through missing paperwork, not through the law. The $124T wealth-transfer statistics ignore it entirely.
first_30_days: With two elder-law attorneys, draft evidence checklists from the state rent-stabilization rules. Run three clinics at senior centers or tenant associations. Charge $199 for the first 20 pilot families and track landlord responses. Publish a plain-language Succession Readiness Score for tenants.

title: Parametric Cover Against Career-Field Collapse
one_liner: Index-based protection that pays out when hiring in a specific occupation falls past a threshold, sold first to bootcamps, income-share funds and private student lenders whose job-guarantee promises are now correlated bets on entry-level demand.
customer: Bootcamps with job guarantees, ISA funds, private student lenders and university tuition-protection programs. Later, workers via employers and universities as a benefit.
problem: These institutions underwrite outcomes assuming stable entry-level demand. If CS, marketing or analytics hiring drops 30% they all fail together, and no hedge exists. The tail risk is now visible (22-25-year-olds in exposed jobs 19% below trend, junior tech postings down ~35% in major EU countries in 2024).
solution: Phase 1 (about 6 months): publish an Occupation Demand Index (postings, hires, claims mix by occupation and metro) plus stress-test analytics, sold as a subscription to lenders and ISA funds. Phase 2: structure parametric covers through an MGA, fronting carrier and reinsurers, triggered by the index. Phase 3: consumer livelihood cover via employers and universities.
why_now: Occupation-level posting data (e.g. Indeed Hiring Lab) is rich, AI exposure is a new correlated risk, parametric insurance infrastructure has matured, ISA funds and bootcamps are under strain, and event-contract markets are normalised.
revenue_model: Analytics subscriptions ($30-120k a year) first, then premiums and ceding commissions.
non_obvious_insight: Occupational risk has never been hedged because individual triggers create moral hazard. An index solves that for institutions whose portfolio effectively is the occupation, and AI displacement is exactly the correlated tail that reinsurers price.
first_30_days: Build the index from public BLS and posting data and backtest against bootcamp outcome reports. Pitch 10 ISA funds, bootcamps and private lenders a paid $10-25k stress-test pilot.

title: Cube Receipt: Win LTL Reclass and Reweigh Disputes
one_liner: A 45-second phone-based dimension-and-weight capture at the shipper's dock produces a timestamped, tamper-evident record attached to the BOL, then used to contest LTL carrier reclass and reweigh charges on contingency.
customer: Small and mid-size B2B shippers with $50K-$2M in annual LTL spend (furniture and home-goods makers, craft food and beverage, DTC brands shipping pallets, HVAC and parts distributors), plus small brokers who arrange LTL and absorb the adjustments when customers refuse to pay.
problem: The NMFC update on July 19, 2025 moved a large number of item numbers to density-based classification. Carriers reweigh and re-dimension freight at terminals with automated dimensioners and bill the corrected class, commonly a $30-$75 fee plus a 20-50% rate uplift. The shipper has no evidence of what actually left the dock, so the carrier's inspection is judge and jury. Most shippers just pay, and brokers who booked the load eat a share when the customer will not.
solution: A mobile app (iPhone LiDAR or camera) walks the packer through a pallet capture: dimensions with a reference marker, weight from a scale photo or entry, density and class check, wrap-bulge and overhang warnings, then hash and timestamp. It generates a QR sticker and a PDF appended to the BOL. When an adjustment invoice arrives (ingested from carrier emails or the freight audit feed), it auto-files the dispute with the evidence, tracks the carrier response, and takes a share of money recovered. It also flags pre-shipment problems, such as stretch-wrap bulge and pallet lip that inflate carrier-measured cube.
why_now: The July 2025 NMFC density shift is still generating adjustment invoices in 2026, and shippers are still learning the new classes. Phone LiDAR is ubiquitous, and carrier dimensioners are now the default at terminals, which makes source-side evidence the missing counterweight.
revenue_model: 25-30% of recovered adjustment charges (contingency), or $99-$299/month per dock. White-label to brokers at about $0.75 per shipment.
non_obvious_insight: Reclass is an evidence-asymmetry game, not a classification problem. The carrier's dimensioner records at the terminal and the shipper has nothing from the source. Terminal cube often includes bulging wrap and the pallet lip. A record made at tender time beats an after-the-fact photo inside the dispute window. Brokers see this daily in adjustment invoices but treat it as a cost of doing business rather than a product.
first_30_days: Approach 10 brokers who place LTL for small shippers. Each has adjustment invoices sitting in AR. Take six months of them, run manual disputes on contingency using whatever photos the shippers have, and log win rates by carrier. Build a no-code capture form (photo checklist plus timestamp) and put it on 3 shippers' docks. Use the win-rate data to sell the app.

title: Billable Legacy Circles for Advance Care Planning
one_liner: Community 'legacy circles' where older adults tell their life stories and finish their advance directives, with a clinician in the room to bill the Medicare advance-care-planning visit.
customer: Medicare Advantage plans and ACOs chasing advance-care-planning quality measures (paying per completed and documented ACP), plus adults 60+ paying about $79-99 for the circle and a keepsake legacy book.
problem: The longevity industry sells more years but says nothing about what they are for, while the 65+ population is peaking and lonely. Advance care planning has had Medicare billing codes for years (99497/99498), yet few eligible people have one, because it is framed as paperwork about death and clinicians have no time. The meaning conversation people actually want is unbilled, and the billable one is avoided.
solution: A 4-session circle of 6-8 people in libraries, churches and senior centers covers values, life story (dignity-therapy style prompts) and what a good ending looks like. Each participant then has a 30-minute individual ACP visit with an NP or social worker under a billing clinician, who files the health-care proxy or POLST. AI transcription and editing produce a 'legacy book' or short video for family. Plans get documented ACPs and engagement data, and participants get a keepsake and a group of peers.
why_now: About 4M Americans turn 65 each year through 2027, so demand is at a peak. Advantage plans are under margin and Star-rating pressure and want cheap, measurable gap-closing. AI transcription and editing make personalized legacy artifacts cheap. Longevity and GLP-1 hype have surfaced the 'healthspan for what' question.
revenue_model: ACP visit billing (about $85-100 per 99497 under Medicare), per-completion fees from MA plans and ACOs, $79-99 participant fee for the circle and legacy book, and sponsorship by estate-planning and elder-law firms.
non_obvious_insight: Advance care planning fails because it is sold as death admin and done alone. Framed as a legacy-building group with a keepsake, participants pull themselves in. The billing code is the boring spine that lets a community and meaning program be paid by a health plan. The group covers the reflection, and the individual visit, not the group, is what gets billed.
first_30_days: Recruit one NP or LCSW (with a supervising physician) and two host venues, such as a public library and a church. Run three circles at $79 and produce sample legacy books. Take the results to the quality lead of one MA plan or ACO that publishes an ACP gap list. Confirm payer-specific billing rules with a compliance advisor before billing anything.

title: Private Road Agreements That Save Rural Closings
one_liner: A flat-fee e-sign-and-record service that produces the road-maintenance and shared-well agreements lenders demand, then turns each road into a dues-collecting association.
customer: Listing and buyer agents and title/escrow officers in rural and mountain markets (CO, MT, ID, WA, OR, UT, NC/TN mountains, northern New England) pay $400-750 per transaction. Later, the households on each road pay $15-40 a month through the association.
problem: A house on a private road often has no enforceable maintenance agreement, only a handshake among neighbors. FHA, VA, USDA and most conventional underwriters want a recorded, legally enforceable agreement, and similar paper for shared wells, septics and driveways. The appraiser flags the private road and the problem lands on nobody. It surfaces 7-10 days before closing, the neighbors have no reason to cooperate, and the deal slips or dies. Between sales the road decays because nobody can collect dues.
solution: Software plus templated law. (1) Detect private vs public roads from county GIS and identify every benefiting parcel and owner. (2) Use state-specific agreement templates reviewed once by local counsel. (3) Run a multi-party e-sign, remote online notarization and e-recording workflow with a friendly neighbor-outreach script. (4) Add a lender-ready cover letter that answers the standard underwriting condition. (5) Upsell to a formal road association (entity, EIN, bank account, ACH dues billing, reserve tracking, lien rights where state statute allows) and shared well/septic agreements.
why_now: Affordability pushes buyers toward exurban and rural homes, and many of them rely on FHA, VA or USDA financing with strict access rules. Remote online notarization and e-recording are now legal and routine in most states. Counties are refusing to accept new roads into public maintenance. Wildfire-zone insurers and fire districts increasingly care about year-round road access and maintenance.
revenue_model: $495 flat per agreement package, paid by the seller through escrow or by a title partner, plus pass-through recording fees. $250 add-on per shared well, septic or easement agreement. Recurring: $29/month association software plus a payment fee on dues (about 3% + $3 per household per month). Referral fees from title partners.
non_obvious_insight: The road is not the deal-killer. The 4-30 neighbors who each have zero incentive to sign are. So the product is the neighbor-consent workflow, not the document. The other insider fact is that underwriters usually accept a simple recorded agreement signed by a majority of owners with proportional cost shares. You don't need a full HOA. Once a road has bank-account-backed dues, it becomes a sticky recurring customer that nobody else serves.
first_30_days: Pick 2 counties dense with private roads (for example the foothills of Larimer/Boulder CO, or Flathead MT). Pull active listings and cross-match them to county road-class GIS to find listings on private roads. Pay a local real-estate attorney about $2-3k to review one template. Cold-contact those listing agents with a specific message: your listing is on a private road, the lender will ask for this, and we deliver in 7 days. Sign 5 pilots at $495 and 2 title officers as referral partners.

title: Genetic-Resource Provenance Ledger for Bio-AI
one_liner: Track which genetic resources and sequences, physical and digital, feed a company's models and pipelines, so it can prove Nagoya compliance today and estimate Cali Fund exposure tomorrow.
customer: Nature-sourced discovery and AI-model builders, starting with the ABS, sustainability and legal units of large pharma, enzyme, ag, food and cosmetics groups, plus sample-collecting AI biotechs such as those mining plants and microbes.
problem: Trend chain: sequence-trained foundation models (Evo 2 trained on 9.3 trillion nucleotides across the tree of life) and proprietary sampling programs (Basecamp's Trillion Gene Atlas, Enveda's sourcing) make genetic-resource provenance a first-class asset. The Cali Fund (launched Feb 2025) asks large DSI users for roughly 1% of profits or 0.1% of revenue, but had only two contributions totaling $6,000 by August 2026. COP17 (Yerevan, Oct 19-30, 2026) is due to confirm rates and allocation. Nagoya duties for physical samples already exist, and public sequence metadata on origin is sparse. Nobody instruments any of it.
solution: Software plus advisory. Ingest sample logs and training or data manifests. Map accessions to origin metadata, flag ABS status, model Cali Fund exposure scenarios, and generate audit-ready disclosures and a 'DSI provenance statement' for model cards. Broker PIC/MAT permit packages for new sampling. Phase 1 revenue comes from existing Nagoya duties on physical collections.
why_now: COP17 is weeks away, and national DSI rules may move faster than the fund. The fund's weak uptake means the near-term product must be Nagoya and provenance assurance, with DSI as an option that COP17 could harden.
revenue_model: $25-120k annual license or advisory for enterprises, $5-15k per collection-permit package, and one-off audit sprints.
non_obvious_insight: The DSI debate is framed as a tax question, but the scarce asset is the sequence-to-origin map. If COP17 or national laws harden, whoever holds the provenance graph sells compliance to everyone. If they do not, the same graph sells 'clean provenance' assurance to acquirers and pharma partners.
first_30_days: Build a lead magnet: a 'DSI exposure snapshot' of a public training corpus or a company's sequence set. Offer 10 free snapshots to sustainability and legal leads. Recruit 2 sample-collecting AI biotechs with live ABS contracts as design partners. Partner with an ABS law firm.

title: Gate-Risk Radar for Evergreen Private Credit
one_liner: A quarterly shadow NAV and gate-probability score for every non-traded BDC and interval fund, sold to the RIAs and OCIOs who put clients into them.
customer: Independent RIAs and family offices ($100M to $3B AUM) with client money in non-traded BDCs, interval and tender-offer funds, at $400 to $1,500 per month per firm. Secondary buyers are TAMPs and wealth platforms (API license) and 401(k) advisers as alternatives enter defined-contribution plans.
problem: Advisers learn a fund has gated from a sponsor letter after the tender window closes. In Q1 2026 non-traded BDC investors requested about $13.9B and got about $7.4B. Blackstone gated BCRED in June 2026 with about 5% fills, and Q2 requests hit a record 12.4% of NAV with only 38% filled. Reported NAVs are smoothed, and nobody tells an adviser whether the next tender will be pro-rated or what to file.
solution: Ingest the tender-offer filings (window and cap), 10-Q and N-PORT marks, non-accruals and PIK share, listed-BDC discount to NAV, secondary bids on non-traded shares, and loan-index prices. Output three things per fund: (1) shadow NAV against reported NAV, (2) probability that the next tender gates and the expected fill rate, (3) a 'if I request X, expect to receive Y' calculator. Add compliance-ready client letters. Start as a public tracker of about 40 funds, then put the alerts and calculator behind a paywall.
why_now: 2026 is the first year pro-rata gating hit the whole non-traded BDC category. Blue Owl merged a non-traded BDC into its listed sibling under redemption pressure. The August 2025 executive order opening 401(k)s to alternatives is about to push far more retail money into these wrappers. Private-credit blowups in late 2025 turned advisers from curious to scared.
revenue_model: Tiered subscription for advisers, an enterprise API for wealth platforms and TAMPs, and a $250 per-fund 'client-ready due diligence memo' for compliance files.
non_obvious_insight: Pro-rata gating makes over-requesting the dominant strategy. Once investors expect a 14 to 38 cent fill, they file bigger requests than they need, so request size becomes a self-amplifying signal. It overstates true demand but predicts fill rates well. The gap between the listed-BDC discount and reported NAV leads request size by about a quarter. Quants see this as a bank-run game with strategic complements, not a credit-loss story, and nobody in wealth tech models it that way.
first_30_days: Scrape EDGAR tender-offer, 10-Q and N-PORT filings for about 40 funds and publish a free weekly 'gate watch' on LinkedIn and Substack framed as research. DM 100 RIA compliance heads and CIOs. Convert 10 to a $500-per-month pilot and start talks with two wealth-platform data teams.

title: Sole-source price-reasonableness memos from council agenda data
one_liner: A buy-side benchmark built from public council packets showing what other governments pay Tyler, Axon, OpenGov and Flock, sold as the missing price-reasonableness memo for every sole-source renewal.
customer: Finance directors, IT directors, purchasing officers and clerks in cities and counties of 5k-250k renewing proprietary software (ERP, permitting, body cameras, ALPR). They pay $495-$1,500 per renewal brief or $3k/year subscription. Councilmembers who want a sanity check are the second audience.
problem: Vendors keep pricing confidential, and sole-source renewals sail through with no comparison. Steuben County, NY approved a five-year Tyler MUNIS/Enterprise renewal at $287,644 in 2026/27 rising 5% a year to $349,633, and the record shows no benchmarking or alternatives (5-0 vote, July 14, 2026). Danbury, CT renewed OpenGov ($71,490.65) and Tyler MUNIS ($299,274.89) unanimously as sole-source because each vendor 'is the developer of proprietary systems' (Aug 5, 2026). In National City, CA a councilmember balked at a $250,000 Tyler budgeting module ('It is a $250,000'), the public questioned the sole-source, and the council demanded a white paper with precise terms and fees.
solution: Continuously ingest agenda packets from the big agenda platforms (Legistar, Granicus, CivicClerk, CivicPlus AgendaCenter) and use LLM extraction to build a structured contract table: vendor, product, price, term, escalator, termination clause, and normalized unit metrics (per capita, per seat, per officer, per camera). Anyone facing a renewal enters the vendor and product and gets a one-page brief within a day. It gives the comparable set, the median escalator, the clauses other governments got (price caps, termination for convenience, data-export rights) and a draft sole-source price-reasonableness paragraph the purchasing officer can attach to the staff report. Later: optional negotiation support on success fee.
why_now: Multi-year Tyler and other vendor contracts are coming up for renewal in 2026, and budgets are squeezed by federal cost shifts (SNAP admin share rising to 75% in October 2026) and grant uncertainty. Agenda packets are now machine-readable at scale. Cheap LLM extraction turns a decade of scattered PDFs into a price table, which was not economically possible before.
revenue_model: $495-1,500 per renewal brief; $3k/year unlimited briefs for a county; 15% of first-year savings for negotiated renewals. Secondary revenue: a quarterly 'what governments pay' index for councils and state associations of counties.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce item is not the data, it is a price-reasonableness determination. Sole-source is only defensible when the buyer can document that the price is reasonable, and none of these records shows one. The public packets already contain the answer, and every vendor claims pricing is confidential while its own contracts are posted in agenda PDFs. Evidence: Steuben County renewal, no alternatives documented (https://citizenportal.ai/articles/9150000/new-york/steuben-county/finance-secures-fiveyear-renewal-pricing-for-munisenterprise-erp-committee-approves); Danbury sole-source renewals (https://citizenportal.ai/articles/8951200/connecticut/fairfield/danbury-city/board-renews-opengov-and-tyler-munis-contracts-totaling-roughly-370000); National City council asking for the terms and fees (https://citizenportal.ai/articles/9526083/california/san-diego-county/national-city/council-asks-city-manager-for-white-paper-after-tyler-technologies-budgeting-demo). Elko's five-year Axon extension at about $91,200 a year is another comparable data point (https://citizenportal.ai/articles/7804457/nevada/elko-county/elko-city/elko-approves-five-year-axon-contract-for-body-cameras-and-redaction-software-to-clear-backlog).
first_30_days: Scrape agenda packets from 300 mid-size jurisdictions in 2 states and extract about 500 contracts for 5 vendors. Publish a free 'What governments actually pay Tyler' leaderboard to earn inbound. Identify contracts expiring in 6-9 months from the term dates in old packets and email those finance directors a free sample brief. Sell the first 10 briefs at $495. Get 2 governments to attach the memo to a staff report as a proof point.

title: Exit Ramps for Dying AI Platforms
one_liner: A converter plus fixed-price migration service that turns Flowise flows, OpenAI Agent Builder graphs and Assistants API integrations into portable, regression-tested code.
customer: AI automation agencies that have 5-50 client agents built on Flowise, Agent Builder or the Assistants API, and in-house AI teams at SMEs that have no engineer to spare. They pay per migrated agent.
problem: Three AI platforms are being killed within about 90 days. The Assistants API shut down on 26 Aug 2026. Agent Builder shuts down on 30 Nov 2026. Flowise was archived in mid-Aug 2026 and its core team leaves on 31 Aug. Non-technical teams built visual flows they cannot maintain as raw code. A Flowise insider says forkers 'own dependency updates, security patches, and model API churn indefinitely, and the contributor community that used to absorb that work is dispersing.' A commenter says telling non-engineers to maintain a TypeScript codebase 'is not a real answer.'
solution: Build importers for Flowise chatflow JSON, Agent Builder workflow exports and Assistants objects (assistants, threads, vector stores, files). They feed a neutral intermediate representation. Exporters then emit (a) Agents SDK / Responses API code, (b) n8n workflows, (c) Langflow. The differentiator is a parity proof. Historical conversation logs are replayed against old and new stacks, and the agency receives a behavioral-diff report it can send to its client. The output is plain, readable code that a coding agent such as Claude Code can maintain. Flowise itself says developers are moving to coding agents because 'rigid workflow low code approach quickly hits the limit.'
why_now: The Assistants API shutdown (26 Aug 2026), the Agent Builder deadline (30 Nov 2026) and the Flowise archive (Aug 2026) all land in one quarter, which forces spending on a real deadline. Coding agents now make code-first output maintainable by non-experts. Flowise has 55.5k stars and 25k forks, so the stranded installed base is large.
revenue_model: Fixed-price migration of $500-2,500 per agent. An agency plan of $199/mo keeps flows mirrored in the intermediate representation with a nightly 'can I still leave?' test. The free converter CLI is the lead magnet.
non_obvious_insight: The demand is a deadline plus a maintenance gap, not a tooling gap. Evidence: OpenAI's deprecations page gives the Agent Builder shutdown as 30 Nov 2026 and the Assistants API as 26 Aug 2026 (https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/deprecations). Flowise's sunset notice sets the code freeze, the archive and the end of core-team support (https://flowiseai.com/sunset). The GitHub repo shows 55.5k stars, 25k forks and 699 open issues (https://github.com/FlowiseAI/Flowise). The HN thread quotes the 'not a real answer' complaint and notes that OpenAI's own Agent Builder is also going away (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49176920). Agencies that resell agents to clients are the buyers, and they carry portfolio risk that a single hobbyist does not. The parity report is what they sell on to their clients.
first_30_days: Week 1: mine the Flowise Discord, GitHub issues and r/n8n for stranded users. Ship a free 'flowise-to-n8n / Agents SDK' CLI that handles the 3 most common node types. Weeks 2-3: cold-DM 40 agencies and sell 5-10 pilot migrations at $750, prioritizing Agent Builder users before the 30 Nov deadline. Week 4: turn the manual steps in those migrations into automated exporters and publish before/after parity reports as case studies.

title: Escrowed Group Orders for Fandom Imports
one_liner: A group-order platform for K-pop, anime and idol merchandise that escrows money, consolidates freight under formal customs entry, and splits domestic shipping.
customer: Group-order managers (volunteer fans running orders on X, Instagram and Discord) and the fans who join their orders, plus small importers.
problem: US de minimis ended on 29 Aug 2025, so single parcels from Korea can be dutiable. Group orders run on PayPal Friends and Family and trust, and fraud is rife: Korea's police reported foreign-national fraud complaints rising from 5,307 (2023) to 19,907 (2025). Group-order managers personally carry the customs and refund risk.
solution: Managers list an order, participants pay into escrow, we purchase against verified receipts and aggregate into one commercial shipment (broker-filed entry, duties and product-safety rules handled), then split to US addresses with tracking. A reputation score for managers and automatic refunds when an order fails.
why_now: The de minimis change turned informal parcel-splitting into an importer-of-record problem, and scam volume is surging.
revenue_model: A 4-6% escrow fee, a freight and handling margin, and a manager subscription for tools.
non_obvious_insight: The informal fan trust economy has no importer and no escrow. Whoever becomes the compliant importer of record plus payment escrow captures the volume, because managers cannot solve duty on their own.
first_30_days: Partner with 5 mid-size US group-order managers. Run 3 orders end to end through a Korean freight forwarder. Charge the escrow fee and publish a public scam tracker for credibility.

title: Tariff Exposure Radar by House Plan
one_liner: A per-plan bill-of-materials scan that flags the small imported, tariff-exposed slice of inputs, prices the swing and proposes lower-exposure substitutes.
customer: Purchasing managers and owners at regional and mid-size builders (100-2,000 homes a year), remodelers, and building-material dealers. Distribution via home builders associations.
problem: NAHB estimates tariffs add $10,900 per home and Brookings sees about $30B added to residential construction and renovation cost by 2027. Only about 7% of inputs are imported, but they are mostly items with no quick domestic substitute, and reported lumber and steel tariff rates conflict across sources. Builders reprice by gut, sign fixed-price contracts blind, and have no per-plan exposure number.
solution: Ingest plan takeoffs and supplier price lists, map each SKU to country of origin and tariff line, and compute exposure per plan and per option package. Deliver escalation-clause language for buyer and sub contracts, alerts when rates change, substitute suggestions from domestic or alternate-origin catalogs, and a group-buy on substitutes.
why_now: Tariff rates are moving and sources disagree. Builder margins are gone (63% use incentives), so a $10K per-home swing decides whether a plan pencils. Structured plan data is now available from design-automation tools.
revenue_model: $500-2,000 per month per builder. $1,500 one-off plan audits. 2-4% rebate on substituted spend from group buys.
non_obvious_insight: Because most of a house is domestic, the tariff burden is a short list of SKUs, so the right tool is a narrow, boring lookup rather than a global trade-compliance platform. The money is in plan-level re-spec and escalation clauses, not in customs filings.
first_30_days: Offer 10 builders a free top-40 exposed-SKU audit from their last three takeoffs and supplier quotes. Send a one-page report and convert 3 to paid. Get a slot in a regional builders association newsletter.

title: Drone Hub Siting and Permit Intelligence
one_liner: Parcel-level zoning, noise and neighbor-risk scoring, plus done-for-you permit filing, for retailers and drone operators expanding launch hubs.
customer: Real-estate and expansion teams at retailers (Walmart, Lowe's, grocers, pharmacies), drone operators and delivery platforms such as Wing, Zipline and DoorDash, and regional chains entering drone delivery.
problem: Cities cannot regulate flight paths but can regulate launch hubs. Northglenn, for example, requires a special-use permit, a 200 ft residential buffer and no more than 65 dB at the property line. Walmart and Wing plan 270+ sites by 2027 (about 150 stores added in a year), and each is a separate local land-use fight.
solution: An LLM-parsed database of municipal zoning codes and drone ordinances, an acoustic model of hub operations, and parcel scoring (buffer, noise, neighbor density, HOA covenants) that outputs a go/no-go and a permit dossier. Add concierge filing and hearing prep. Also sell a model-ordinance toolkit to city planners.
why_now: Lowe's launched Wing/DoorDash delivery on September 28, 2026, and Walmart's rollout turns hub siting into a mass-production problem. With airspace approvals no longer the binding constraint, zoning boards are. LLMs make parsing thousands of local codes cheap.
revenue_model: $2-5k per site score, $10-25k per permit package, and $50-150k a year in enterprise SaaS. City licenses for the planning toolkit are a smaller add-on.
non_obvious_insight: The sky is federally preempted but the ground is local, so the scaling constraint has moved from the FAA to the zoning board. Whoever owns the ordinance graph decides where drone networks can expand, and both sides of the table will pay.
first_30_days: Scrape and structure drone-relevant ordinances for the top 150 municipalities in one high-growth state. Offer a free top-20 site scoring to a regional grocery or pharmacy chain, convert one paid permit package, and publish a model ordinance to generate city leads.

title: Voice-Clone-Proof Verbal Deals for Grain and Cattle
one_liner: A two-channel confirmation step and verified-payee ledger that makes phone-and-handshake commodity deals safe from cloned voices and redirected payments.
customer: Regional grain elevators and co-ops, livestock auction markets and order buyers, ag input retailers, and the ag lenders that finance them.
problem: Agriculture runs on calls: bids, forward contracts, cattle sales, input prepays and cash rents, with confirmation by email. About 3 seconds of audio can clone a farmer's or merchandiser's voice, and BEC cost $3.05B in 2025. Retail beef hit a record $9.64/lb, contract sizes are up, and farm distress attracts fake-buyer scams. Small operations have no fraud team, and cross-bank recovery through the FBI's process is rarely accessible to them.
solution: Verify each farmer's bank account ownership once, with a passphrase or app approval. Any verbal contract above a threshold, or any change of payee, triggers an out-of-band push approval or a callback to a pre-registered number. Settlement pays only to verified accounts. Integrate with grain accounting and auction-clerk systems. Extend to cash-rent payments to older landlords and to the December input prepay season.
why_now: Voice cloning is mainstream. Chainalysis reports impersonation scams up 1,400% with average payments up 253%, and the FBI's Sept 17 2026 PSA cites AI video calls in law-enforcement impersonation. The December prepay season is about ten weeks away, and record livestock prices raise the stakes.
revenue_model: $300-800 a month per elevator or auction location plus $0.50-2 per verified payment. Lenders pay per portfolio, and cyber insurers may give premium credits.
non_obvious_insight: In agriculture the voice is the credential. Forty-year relationships mean nobody asks for ID, and voice cloning breaks the oldest trust protocol in commodity trading. The paying customer is the elevator or auction, which bears misdirected settlements, not the farmer. The tool plugs into settlement systems that banks cannot see.
first_30_days: Interview 20 elevator merchandisers and controllers. Pilot with 2 regional co-ops during harvest settlements using a bank account-owner check plus text push approval. Present to auction-market clerk groups. Ask a cyber-insurance broker about premium credits. Offer a December prepay fraud drill.

title: Night Shift Tox Bulletin for Opioid Settlement Counties
one_liner: A no-patient-data network where rural ER nurses text in what they are seeing, turned into weekly local drug-supply alerts sold to counties spending opioid settlement money.
customer: County opioid settlement councils and public health departments, EMS medical directors, jails, harm-reduction programs and rural hospitals. Paid by county contract from opioid settlement funds.
problem: New adulterants show up in a rural ER as a pattern before they show up in any dataset. Examples are patients who are sedated but not responding to naloxone, or patients with a slow heart rate and low blood pressure that is not the usual opioid picture, or brutal withdrawal with high blood pressure. Confirmatory lab results take weeks or months. Surveillance networks are concentrated in academic and urban centers, so a rural county may learn about something two states over long after the ER has seen it. Nurses talk to each other in the break room and on private Facebook groups, but they have no safe way to alert the county, EMS, jail or harm-reduction workers. Hospital administrations do not want a nurse speaking for the hospital.
solution: A 30-second SMS or Signal report with no patient identifiers: date, county, number of patients, presentation flags, response to reversal, what the patients said they took, and any new physical findings such as wounds. Reports are aggregated with a minimum threshold (for example 3 or more per week) to protect privacy. The service returns a plain-language weekly county bulletin to nurses, EMS, jail medical staff and harm-reduction groups, and triggers targeted drug-checking or lab testing of residue with a lab partner. Include a jail-specific alert because withdrawal from newer sedatives is dangerous inside a jail.
why_now: Medetomidine, a veterinary sedative, is now in the illicit supply well beyond Philadelphia. Wastewater data showed it in at least one of 14 states every week from October 2025 to January 2026, and California published an emerging issue brief in April 2026. The main ER sentinel program has only about 17 to 20 academic centers, so rural emergency departments are barely covered. Tens of billions of dollars in opioid settlement funds are arriving in local hands, and county councils are actively looking for evidence-based data and surveillance projects.
revenue_model: $12-36k per year per county or multi-county region, with a lower price for small counties and bundled state contracts through state opioid settlement offices. A secondary product is a per-test fee when the network triggers drug-checking or lab confirmation, and a jail early-warning subscription.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce thing is not lab capacity. It is a trusted channel for the person who sees it first and has no authority to speak. A night-shift nurse is a better early-warning sensor than a dashboard, and the data is qualitative and deliberately human: 'this doesn't look like what we normally see.' Because you can build it with no PHI, nurses can contribute from their own phones off shift without touching hospital systems. Other tools (ODMAP, poison center feeds) are built for incident counts and law enforcement or EMS reports, not clinical pattern recognition.
first_30_days: Recruit 25 rural ER and night nurses from state nurses' groups and private Facebook communities. Send a free weekly bulletin to three neighboring counties and their EMS agencies. Attend an opioid settlement council meeting (agendas and minutes are public) in one of them. Offer a paid six-month pilot at $1,000 per month. Line up one lab partner for confirmatory testing. Get a lawyer to review the no-PHI reporting language and publish a clear policy telling nurses to leave out anything identifiable.

title: Rights-Cleared 1929-1963 Corpus for AI
one_liner: Join scanned mid-century books, magazines and newspapers to Copyright Office renewal records to produce provably public-domain text for AI training, with libraries paid a share and spared the scraper load.
customer: AI labs, foundation-model startups and fine-tuning shops that need litigation-proof training data, plus library and archive partners who supply scans (buyer is head of data or general counsel).
problem: Clean training data is now a legal necessity, but the best public-domain corpus (Harvard's Institutional Books 1.0, 983,004 volumes, 242B tokens) is largely pre-1929 text. For US works published 1929-1963, copyright lapsed unless renewed, yet renewals were rare (a 1961 Copyright Office study found fewer than 15% of registered copyrights renewed). The registration and renewal records exist but nobody has joined them to scanned text at scale. Meanwhile libraries are drowning in AI bots and have no sustainable way to offer their collections.
solution: Take scans that already exist (Internet Archive, partner libraries, HathiTrust-style holdings). Match each volume to Catalog of Copyright Entries registrations and renewals (Stanford renewal database for 1923-1949 books; Copyright Office online records for 1950+), and exclude foreign works restored under the URAA. Output a per-volume rights dossier with evidence links and a confidence score. Sell dataset snapshots with a signed provenance certificate (and insurance-backed warranty as revenue grows). Offer participating libraries a paid bulk-snapshot mirror (S3 or rsync) so AI buyers stop scraping their sites, with a revenue share.
why_now: The Authors Guild v. OpenAI/Microsoft unsealed briefs (2026-09-27) claim executives knew mass book piracy was illegal. Harvard and OpenAI/Microsoft-backed public-domain releases show buyers want clean data. Creative Commons (Aug 2026) says heritage institutions need standardized 'prosocial conditions' for AI access, and some (the National Library of the Netherlands, Trove) have closed access.
revenue_model: Dataset licenses ($25k-$250k per slice or annual refresh), provenance certificate fees, revenue share paid to libraries, bespoke rights-clearance projects for publishers reissuing out-of-print titles.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck for legal AI text isn't scanning, it's rights determination: a huge band of 1929-1963 US works is public domain because nobody filed a renewal, and it's invisible until someone does the record join at scale. Libraries currently do this by hand. Evidence: Institutional Books 1.0 covers 983,004 volumes and 242B tokens (https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.08300). Wikipedia notes non-renewed pre-1964 works are public domain, the 1961 study, and the databases that hold the records (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copyright_renewal). GLAM-E Lab survey: 39 of 43 institutions (91%) saw traffic surges, 69% of those blamed AI training bots, 74% deployed countermeasures, and robots.txt was largely ignored (https://glamelab.org/products/are-ai-bots-knocking-cultural-heritage-offline/). Creative Commons Aug 2026 on institutions closing access (https://creativecommons.org/2026/08/19/open-heritage-in-the-age-of-artificial-intelligence/). Authors Guild briefs, HN 626 points (https://authorsguild.org/news/ag-v-openai-top-execs-knew-mass-book-piracy-was-illegal/).
first_30_days: Days 1-10: pick a narrow, high-value slice (for example 1950-1963 US trade, technical and hobby magazines where renewal was nearly nonexistent) and download the matching Internet Archive scans and renewal records. Days 10-25: run a first 5,000-volume join, have a copyright attorney sign off on the method and the URAA exclusions, and publish a free 500-volume sample with dossiers. Days 25-30: send the sample to 15 AI data buyers and licensed-data startups and to 5 mid-size libraries for a mirror pilot. Target one paid pilot in 90 days.

title: Shared Apprentice Pools for Office Work
one_liner: A group-training organisation (the Australian trades model) for white-collar work. It employs new grads, trains them to supervise AI output, and rotates them across several mid-size hosts that share the cost and get first pick.
customer: Mid-size (100-2,000 employee) accounting firms, insurance brokerages, property managers, logistics and healthcare-admin employers pay host fees. The new grads are W-2 employees of the pool.
problem: Each employer rationally stops hiring juniors because AI absorbs junior tasks and trained juniors get poached. Collectively that empties the 3-5-year-experience pipeline around 2029. Stanford finds 22-25-year-olds in exposed jobs 19% below trend, and 42% of recent grads are underemployed.
solution: The pool hires 25-40 juniors per cohort and gives 8 weeks of workflow-specific training (AI-assisted bookkeeping, claims triage, contract abstraction). It then places them 2-3 days a week across up to three hosts for $38-50/hr as supervised AI-assist analysts with QA metrics. Senior mentors get stipends, and hosts pay a fixed conversion fee at months 12-18. The pool handles payroll, insurance and HR.
why_now: The freeze is widening (Aug 2026 Stanford revision), and AI tools make a trained junior productive from week two. Employers are stuck in a prisoner's-dilemma on training. Pooled employment is a proven fix in Australian trades and in Germany's dual system.
revenue_model: Host fees at 25-35% gross margin, plus conversion fees of $8-15k per hire.
non_obvious_insight: The junior freeze is a coordination failure (a training externality), not a technology fact. Hosts are buying a cheap call option on the scarce 2029 mid-level hire, and pooling removes the poaching fear that blocks individual employers.
first_30_days: Pick one vertical with retiring owner-operators (independent insurance brokerages or small CPA firms). Sign 6 hosts at a pilot rate through a state society or trade association. Hire 10 grads via college career centres. Use a PEO for payroll so you build no HR infrastructure.

title: Tariff Refund Claim Files for Small Importers
one_liner: Turn a small importer's messy customs data into a refund-ready, financeable claim ledger, paid by success fee or on sale of the claim.
customer: US importers of record with roughly $50K to $5M of IEEPA duties who lack in-house customs staff, plus the licensed customs brokers serving them. Claim-buying funds and lenders are the second payer, paying a per-file diligence fee.
problem: The Supreme Court struck down the IEEPA tariffs in February 2026 and the CIT ordered refunds. CBP's CAPE tool has accepted about $134.7B of the roughly $166B pool as of September 11, 2026. The tail sits with the smallest importers. Their ACE accounts are unapproved, they missed the 90-day request window, or their entries are liquidated beyond the 80-day reprocessing window, which the DOJ is appealing at the Federal Circuit. Phase 3, for liquidated entries, was slated for October 6 but delayed. Many are selling claims at deep discounts out of fear or confusion.
solution: Ingest ACE entry-summary reports, broker CSVs and payment records. Map every line to the IEEPA HTS 9903 lines. Compute per-entry phase eligibility, liquidation dates and protest deadlines. Flag duplicate or wrong importer-of-record entries, drawback and FTZ overlaps, and interest owed. Output CAPE-ready batches plus a chain-of-title 'claim data room' with a probability-weighted value for the appeal-dependent entries. A licensed broker partner files, so the product stays software plus workflow. The same engine reprocesses future tariff refunds and exclusions.
why_now: The window is open now: CAPE phases run through fall 2026, the Federal Circuit appeal will set the value of the liquidated tail, and hedge funds and lenders are already buying refund claims. Successor tariffs under other statutes create the same entry-level data problem next year.
revenue_model: 8 to 12% success fee on refunds recovered. A 2 to 4% origination fee when a claim is sold or financed. $500 to $2,000 per-claim diligence files sold to buyers. A subscription for customs brokers who use it across their book.
non_obvious_insight: Distressed-claims desks (Lehman, FTX, Celsius trade claims) know a claim's price is set less by the underlying merits than by documentation quality, chain of title and timing. Whoever standardizes the data room becomes the market's gatekeeper. The small-importer tail is mispriced because sellers can't prove what they are owed, and buyers can't underwrite what they can't verify. The moat is the underwriting file, not the filing.
first_30_days: Build an ES-003 and ACE CSV parser with two or three friendly licensed customs brokers. Offer a free 'refund gap audit' to 30 small importers found through public importer lists. Sign 10 on contingency. Get letters of intent from one or two claim buyers wanting standardized diligence files.

title: Task-Shifting Engine for Tech-Led Vet Visits
one_liner: Standing-order templates, scheduling and a state-by-state supervision rules database that let clinics move routine care from vets to technicians and, soon, VPAs, without breaking practice acts.
customer: Independent clinics adopting a team-based model, multi-state clinic groups, and VPA-employing practices. Later: PIMS and telehealth vendors licensing the rules API.
problem: Vet supply is nearly flat (91,100 vets; about 3,100 openings a year) while techs are scarce (about 2 per vet versus a 4:1 ideal, with most leaving within 4 years). The team-based model is how affordable clinics reach invoices about 44% below average, yet PIMS scheduling is built around doctor visits. Nobody supplies compliant protocols for who may do what under which supervision in each state.
solution: A library of 'tech appointment' types (booster vaccines, rechecks, suture removal, senior lab draws, weight programs, dental prep) with standing orders, consent scripts and a DVM sign-off queue. A versioned rules database maps each task to state supervision levels, with alerts when boards change rules, and audit logs show who did what under whose supervision. A scheduling plug-in books the right role and length.
why_now: Colorado State is launching an MS for the new VPA license (dogs and cats, supervised, routine surgery and tests), and it has been more than a decade in the making. Roll-ups now span many states, and clinics need to raise output per DVM. AI scribes and agents are generating plans that implicitly delegate tasks.
revenue_model: $199-399 per clinic per month for templates and scheduling; $500-5K per month for rules API and multi-state groups; VPA program design consulting.
non_obvious_insight: A new professional tier shifts value to whoever holds the rules and the protocols. In human health, scope-of-practice changes (NPs, PAs) spawned decades of compliance and protocol software. Vet medicine is at the start of that curve, and the rules database is the moat while templates are the wedge.
first_30_days: With a vet-law attorney, build a matrix of 10 states by about 40 tasks from statutes and board rules. Publish a free 'Can my tech do this?' checker in vet-tech communities. Pilot the appointment templates in 5 clinics and aim to sell 3 multi-state groups on the rules feed.
